Jennifer Lawrence
By Kathryn Shattuck
Jennifer Lawrence, who is shooting “Passengers,” a deep-space romance with Chris Pratt in Atlanta, thought she had overslept when her assistant burst into her room this morning.
But no, she was merely delivering word of Ms. Lawrence’s fourth Oscar nomination and her third for best actress — this time for her portrayal of the title character in “Joy,” based in part on Joy Mangano, inventor of the Miracle Mop.
“I’ve been working so I didn’t know that nominations were out,” Ms. Lawrence said nonchalantly. “I think that’s the way to do it.”
But don’t assume she’s blasé as she racks up Streepian acclaim in seemingly every role she touches. (“Don’t say that — it’s not every movie!” she scolded good-naturedly.)
“I’m very happy,” Ms. Lawrence reassured us, sounding exactly that.
“Joy,” her third collaboration with the director David O. Russell, and the actors Robert De Niro and Bradley Cooper, belongs, “almost entirely to Ms. Lawrence,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times, “She is the kind of movie star who turns everyone else into a character actor.”
“This is not a complaint but an acknowledgment of both her charisma and her generosity,” he clarified, perhaps unnecessarily.
Never mind that she’d do anything with Mr. Russell. The realization that “all of us have something of hers in our house” sealed the deal to play Ms. Mangano, Ms. Lawrence said. “It’s a great story and told at a really cool time when we’re trying to figure out where working women belong in society.”
(Ms. Lawrence of course has
weighed in
on an issue of importance to working women – gender pay inequality – in an essay for Lena Dunham’s newsletter Lenny.)
Before heading to the set, Ms. Lawrence pondered the films and performances that captured her attention this year: “Spotlight,” “The Big Short” and “The Danish Girl,” which she had just seen last night.
“I always watch people who can do these period films in awe, and I thought Alicia Vikander was phenomenal,” she said of the best supporting actress nominee. (Ms. Lawrence’s fellow nominees are Cate Blanchett, Brie Larson, Charlotte Rampling and Saoirse Ronan.)
O.K., maybe Ms. Lawrence sounded a tiny bit jaded when she admitted that she didn’t have any major Oscar revelry planned. But sometimes all a working woman really wants is an evening to herself.
“I will come home and have a glass of wine and watch repeats of ‘Veep,’” Ms. Lawrence said before bounding off. “And that’s celebratory enough for me.”
Sylvester Stallone
By Cara Buckley
Pacing back and forth, back and forth, in his bathroom in the predawn darkness
Thursday
, an anxious and jet-lagged Sylvester Stallone tried but failed to not watch the Oscar nominations on TV.
He had left straight from the Golden Globes
on Sunday
– where he won best supporting actor for his performance as Rocky in “Creed’”– to fly across the Atlantic for the film’s London premiere.
After another trans-Atlantic flight, he slipped back into his house at
4 a.m.
, an hour and a half before the Academy’s nominations were to be announced on the West Coast. He vowed not to wake his wife and paced for a bit, then finally flicked on the TV.
The names for best supporting actor nominees were read, as is the norm, alphabetically, and Mr. Stallone, who is 69, marveled at the nominees’ youth and vitality. (Mark Rylance, the second oldest, is 55. The other contenders are Christian Bale, Tom Hardy and Mark Ruffalo.)
“Everyone here is a star,” Mr. Stallone said he thought to himself, “These guys are the real deal.” He’d already convinced himself an Oscar nomination was probably not in the cards. “I figured I’d gotten my just due at the Golden Globes,” he said, “And I didn’t think that was ever going to happen.”
After his name was announced
last on the list,
he shook awake his wife, Jennifer Flavin. The first and last time Mr. Stallone was nominated for an Oscar was for “Rocky” nearly 30 years ago. (He received two nominations then, for actor and best original screenplay, but lost in both categories.)
“I appreciated it, but didn’t understand how incredibly competitive and difficult it was,” he said.
Mr. Stallone said he wasn’t sure why exactly he had been nominated this time, nor why there was so much goodwill toward him. (For his Golden Globe win, he received a standing ovation.) “Why do you think that is?” he asked. “Is it because I’ve just been hanging around long enough?”
Another upside of “Creed,” he said, was that his three daughters – ages 13, 17 and 19 – finally wanted to watch a movie he had starred in.
“They never got into the intellectual musings or the gentle humor of Rambo,” he said. “They told me, ‘Finally, we understand some of what you’re saying. Some.’”
Alicia Vikander
By Kathryn Shattuck
Alicia Vikander, the prolific Swedish actress, was up before dawn in Las Vegas, preparing to shoot the latest “Bourne” installment, when she decided to check in on the Oscar nominations.
But as soon as the supporting actress category came up, her Wi-Fi broke down. “The frame just stopped, and I was like, ‘Oh my God, what happened?’” she said. “Then my phone starting ringing, and I was almost afraid to pick it up.”
What happened, Ms. Vikander learned, was that she had been nominated for her role as Gerda, the wife of Einar Wegener (who came to be known as Lili Elbe), one of the first people to undergo sex reassignment surgery, in “The Danish Girl,” set in 1926 Copenhagen. (Eddie Redmayne, who plays Einar, was nominated as well.)
In a year in which critics had their pick of
several quietly incandescent performances
from Ms. Vikander — among them, the protofeminist British pacifist Vera Brittain in “Testament of Youth” and Ava, the exquisite embodiment of artificial intelligence in “Ex Machina” — it was as Gerda who shone brightest.
“She is called upon to support the man she loves as he erases himself from her life,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times, adding that she “acts from the inside out, with an openness and spontaneity that is especially rare in movies like this one.”
But on Thursday morning, the publicly reserved Ms. Vikander was all bubbles during a quick phone call, her throaty laughter sounding like so much Champagne.
“I’m very, very good,” she practically gushed of her first Oscar nod. “When I saw the names that were nominated, I felt so humbled to be included alongside such an amazing group of actors.” (Her fellow nominees are Jennifer Jason Leigh, Rooney Mara, Rachel McAdams and Kate Winslet.)
So how would she be celebrating? By congratulating two other new nominees: Matt Damon, her “Bourne” co-star, who was nominated for “The Martian,” and — just a hunch, because she craftily whizzed off to work before answering — Michael Fassbender (“Steve Jobs”), with whom she was spotted holding hands at the Golden Globes.
But before hanging up, she managed to squeeze in her own picks of 2015: the film “Spotlight,” about The Boston Globe’s investigation into the sexual abuse of children by priests, and Charlotte Rampling, for what Ms. Vikander called “an amazing performance” in “45 Years.”
Mark Rylance
By Steven McElroy
When it comes to the Academy Awards, Mark Rylance is much more keen on being up for an Oscar than on the prospect of actually taking home the trophy on Feb. 28.
“I find it uncomfortable winning, but being nominated I really like because you’re usually listed with a really wonderful group of actors,” he said in a brief interview moments after the nominations were announced. He hadn’t watched the announcement – a publicist gave him the news – and didn’t yet know who else was nominated. (His competitors are Christian Bale, Tom Hardy, Mark Ruffalo and Sylvester Stallone.)
Speaking by phone from Boston, where he is rehearsing “Nice Fish,” which begins previews on Sunday at
American Repertory Theater
, Mr. Rylance said he was pleased if not entirely surprised – a point he somehow expressed with humility – by the nomination for best supporting actor for his role in the Steven Spielberg thriller “
Bridge of Spies
.” Mr. Rylance, 55, plays the historical character
Rudolf Abel
, a Soviet spy.
To research the role, Mr. Rylance said, he found as much information as he could, including YouTube videos of Abel being arrested. He studied Abel’s look and walk, but may not have quite nailed the accent.
“People said he sounded Scottish so I went with that, but then I bumped into Sting, after we’d made the film unfortunately, and Sting was the first man I met who knew Rudolf Abel. He knew him because Abel grew up in Newcastle where Sting grew up. Sting was very adamant that I needed to sound Geordie, which is the Newcastle dialect,” he said. “I ended up apologizing.”
This is Mr. Rylance’s first Oscar nomination, though he has won plenty of accolades for his stage work. That includes three Tony Awards, and he’s known for some odd acceptance speeches. Twice
he has used loopy poems by Louis Jenkins
, a Minnesota writer whose work is actually the source material for “Nice Fish.”
He likes being a nominee better in part because “winning moves into a surreality of winning something over someone like Al Pacino,” he said, which is what happened when Mr. Rylance won a 2011 Tony for “Jerusalem,” and Mr. Pacino was up for “The Merchant of Venice.”
“I’d prefer really that the person who gets up is just the nominated speaker for the five nominees,” Mr. Rylance said. “Rather than the game being who’s the winner, the game would just be who’s going to be the one who’s deemed to be the right person to speak on behalf of these five wonderful actors.”

Some of the festivities were
broadcast
live on the Italian state broadcaster, RAI, on Tuesday morning, following newspaper articles
celebrating her age
. And journalists, photographers, relatives and researchers crowded into her tiny two-room apartment in Pallanza, a picturesque Italian town on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore.
Birthday greetings came by way of elementary school children who sent poster-size cards; sundry town officials; and President Sergio Mattarella, who wished her “serenity and good health” on behalf of all Italians.

“She’s very, very happy,” said her niece Maria Antonietta Sala, whose mother, Angela — Emma’s sister — died at 102.
Her Secret to Longevity
I wrote about Ms. Morano two years ago, when she was only 115, and she told me she believed that her secret to longevity was eating
three raw eggs a day and remaining single
.
Ms. Morano has no doubts about how she made it this long: Her elixir for longevity consists of raw eggs, which she has been eating — three per day — since her teens when a doctor recommended them to counter anemia. She is also convinced that being single for most of her life, after an unhappy marriage that ended in 1938 following the death of an infant son, has kept her kicking. Separation was rare then, and divorce became legal in
Italy
only in 1970. She said she had plenty of suitors after that, but never chose another partner. “I didn’t want to be dominated by anyone,” she said.
Ms. Morano, who has cut back to two eggs a day, lives a very simple life. She has been homebound for some years, and her diet remains Spartan, if unorthodox: In addition to eggs, she eats bananas and ladyfinger cookies.
She recently cut meat from her diet, “because she got it into her mind that it could lead to a tumor, so she stopped eating it,” said Ms. Sala, who helps look after her aunt, along with two caregivers.

The best music festivals don’t strive to offer something for everybody. They go deep, programming live performances like a set by an inspired disc jockey, where each selection responds to and illuminates the rest. Grimes
, Miike Snow, Gary Numan, Blood Orange, Laurie Anderson, Odesza, the Orb and Oneohtrix Point Never, along with electronic-music pioneers, songwriters, producers, composers and D.J.s. Geeky and proud of it, Moogfest has symposiums on topics like Afro-Futurism and Transhumanism, as well as “Durationals” — experimental performances by musicians like the rocker EMA — and technology-minded art installations, including one that plans to “repurpose old telephone switchboards into working modular synthesizers.”

Big Ears Festival
, in Knoxville, Tenn., March 31-April 1, shares some headliners with Moogfest: Laurie Anderson, the Sun Ra Arkestra and the band Sunn O))). Other performers are just as varied, among them the jazz saxophonists Kamasi Washington and Anthony Braxton, the songwriter Angel Olsen, the 1970s Krautrock experimenters Faust and the Knoxville Symphony playing Philip Glass; John Luther Adams; and, from the National, Bryce Dessner. Fans of Lou Reed’s
“Metal Machine Music”
can hear live drones created with his original setup. Implicit in the lineup is the idea that at their more daring fringes, styles and genres melt into an impulse toward the incantatory and ecstatic.
An intriguing new festival is taking shape in Cuba — specifically the city of Santiago de Cuba, a center of deep Afro-Cuban lore that will host
Manana 2016
, May 4-6. Produced by British expats and a Cuban rapper, the festival is an encounter between Santiago’s folkloric groups — playing rumba, son montuno, guaracha and other Afro-Cuban traditions — and electronic dance music, primarily from British rhythm explorers like Quantic (Will Holland, who’s based in Colombia), Plaid and A Guy Called Gerald. It’s likely to catalyze flesh-and-computer collaborations that couldn’t happen anywhere else.

It’s a little bizarre this political season to see wealthy candidates in both parties denouncing our political system for representing mostly the interests of, well, wealthy people.
Bizarre, perhaps, and sometimes a tad hypocritical, but also accurate. America’s political system
is
rigged. The deck
is
stacked against ordinary people. That’s the frustration that has fueled, in very different ways, the anti-establishment campaigns of Donald Trump, Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in particular, and that is leading other candidates, like Hillary Clinton, to grab their pitchforks as well.
“Yes, the economy is rigged in favor of those at the top,”
Clinton declared
in the Democratic debate last week.
One glimpse of the structural unfairness in America is this: A dumb rich kid is now more likely to graduate from college than a smart poor kid, according to Robert Putnam of Harvard University.
Another: The 20 wealthiest Americans, a group that would fit comfortably inside a luxury private jet bound for a private Caribbean island, are worth more than the poorer half of the American population, according to
a recent report
from the Institute for Policy Studies. Forbes’s wealthiest 100 are worth as much as all 42 million African-Americans, the report says.
“Correctly, we suspect that the system is rigged, our government has become coin-operated and that we’ve been sidelined,” Wendell Potter and Nick Penniman write in their eye-opening new book about money in politics, “
Nation on the Take
.” They call for a “profound course correction,” like those the United States has periodically undertaken before.
So it’s healthy for American voters to be demanding change. But when societies face economic pain, they sometimes turn to reforms, and other times to scapegoats (like refugees this year). So the historic question for 2016 is which direction the popular revolt among American voters will ultimately take. A President Trump or President Cruz would build walls and
waterboard suspected terrorists
, a President Clinton or President Sanders would raise the minimum wage and invest in at-risk children.
It seems to me to make more sense to target solutions than scapegoats, but sense is often in short supply in politics. After a characteristically brilliant speech by Adlai Stevenson, the Democratic nominee for president in 1952 and 1956, a supporter is said to have bellowed, “Every thinking American will vote for you!”
Legend has it that Stevenson shouted back: “That’s not enough. I need a majority!”
In the solutions domain, a starting point should be to reduce the influence of money in politics.
The pharmaceutical industry, for example, has used
its lobbying heft
— it spent $272,000 in campaign donations per member of Congress last year, and it has more lobbyists than there are members of Congress — to bar the government from bargaining for drug prices in Medicare. That amounts to a $50 billion annual gift to pharmaceutical companies.
The rise of inequality has complex roots, and some aren’t easily solved. For example, the empowerment of women, coupled with the tendency of people to marry those like themselves, means that high-earning men increasingly pair with high-earning women to form super-high-earning families.

Paul Piff, a social psychologist, has
conducted experiments

In this election season, many Americans feel that they are living that rigged Monopoly game.
Two business school professors, Michael Norton and Dan Ariely,

So may the insurrection gain ground but be channeled not by punishing scapegoats, but by pursuing reforms that make the system work better for ordinary Americans.
